idiom_name: Response data + renderer class per media type (JSONRenderer, TemplateHTMLRenderer)
implementation_notes: Stage one is a format-independent data structure: the view returns Response(content) where content is plain Python data (or serialiser output) carrying no rendering decisions. Stage two is the renderer class: Django REST Framework performs content negotiation on the request, selects the renderer and turns that intermediate representation into the final byte stream - the wording Django uses for its own rendering process - with JSONRenderer, TemplateHTMLRenderer/StaticHTMLRenderer and the browsable API as ready channels and a documented BaseRenderer contract for new ones. Keep one renderer per channel, order renderer_classes deliberately because the first class wins for an unspecified Accept header, and pass a dict context to the HTML channel instead of pre-rendered markup. What replaces the classic DOM-plus-stylesheet structure is exactly this: plain data plus a renderer class, with no logical document object to maintain; the classic form is still justified only for document pipelines where the page must also be published as XML (see the sibling lxml variant).
pitfalls: Renderer order decides the default channel: with Accept: */* the first class in renderer_classes wins, so a reordering silently changes what clients receive.
TemplateHTMLRenderer uses response.data as the template context, so returning a serialiser instance instead of a dict renders an object repr rather than the page.
Renderer classes belong to the view, not the data: putting channel logic in the serialiser couples the logical page to one output format and defeats the second stage.

variants.name: lxml element tree + XSLT stylesheet per channel
variants.idiom_name: lxml.etree logical page + etree.XSLT stylesheet per channel
variants.implementation_notes: The literal pattern in Python: build the logical page as an lxml.etree tree (or parse it from the value objects), compile one XSLT stylesheet per channel with etree.XSLT once, and render by applying it to that tree - lxml supports XPath 1.0, XSLT 1.0 and EXSLT through libxml2/libxslt. Compile stylesheets at start-up and reuse them, keep the page free of presentation attributes, and treat the stylesheet as code: libxslt resolves entities and reaches the file system, so never apply a user-supplied stylesheet. Choose this variant for document pipelines where the same page must also be published as XML or fed to a PDF/XSL-FO formatter; for ordinary web responses the framework renderer variant is simpler.
variants.code_sketch:
from lxml import etree

page = etree.XML("<invoice total='42.00'><customer>ACME</customer></invoice>")  # stage 1
render_html = etree.XSLT(etree.parse("invoice-html.xsl"))   # compiled once
html = str(render_html(page))                                 # stage 2: HTML channel
# render_fo = etree.XSLT(etree.parse("invoice-fo.xsl")) -> XSL-FO -> PDF formatter
pitfalls: XSLTResultTree keeps a reference to its source tree, so caching results (or strings derived from them) can pin the whole page in memory.
The standard library's xml.etree has no XSLT at all: code written against lxml.etree silently loses the renderer if the project standardises on the stdlib module.
libxslt has no sandbox - untrusted stylesheets can read files and consume CPU/memory - and entity resolution must be disabled explicitly when parsing untrusted pages.
